title: CVE-2026-124284 - Genetec Security Center Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
CVE-2026-16663 - Pre-authentication out-of-bounds write in MCUboot encrypted serial recovery image decryption
text:
8.4

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-16663
Pre-authentication out-of-bounds write in MCUboot encrypted serial recovery image decryption

MCUboot's encrypted serial-recovery path contains an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write in decrypt_region_inplace() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c. The routine decrypts an uploaded encrypted image one flash sector at a time into a sector-sized stack VLA buf[sz], but when the current sector is still inside the image header it sets the destination index to the absolute header size (idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size; at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:156) and then decrypts into &buf[idx]. The correct sibling routine boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:876 uses the sector-relative idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size - abs_off; the serial path is missing the - abs_off term, so for any sector after the first the index runs past the end of the stack buffer.

The ih_hdr_size field is a uint16_t taken verbatim from the uploaded image header. On the second sector onward, when ih_hdr_size exceeds the sector size, &buf[idx] points beyond buf and boot_enc_decrypt() writes attacker-controlled plaintext into adjacent stack frames. The path is reached pre-authentication: bs_upload() calls boot_handle_enc_fw() (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c:1208) after upload, and the pre-decryption signature gate in decrypt_image_inplace() is compiled out (#if 0 at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:226-233), so the header is never validated before decryption.

A second error in the same window computation affects the first sector. When a sector holds both the end of the header and the start of the TLV area, the decrypt length is clamped to tlv_off - (off + bytes_copied), measured from the start of the sector rather than from idx (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:166). An encrypted image whose header and payload end within the first sector is therefore decrypted for ih_hdr_size bytes more than it should be: into the TLV area and, when the image ends near the end of the sector, past buf. This form needs no oversized header, so even an ordinary small encrypted image can trigger it, and it reaches devices with sectors of up to about 128 KiB rather than only those whose sector is smaller than the 16-bit ih_hdr_size.

Reaching the sink requires a build with MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES and serial recovery enabled, and access to the device's serial/USB recovery interface (unauthenticated by design). With the public-key encryption schemes the AES content key is wrapped to the device's public encryption key, so an attacker can author a fully crafted encrypted image — including a malicious ih_hdr_size — without the image-signing private key. The result is a controllable stack memory-corruption inside the bootloader before any signature check, providing a path to code execution in the secure-boot root of trust that bypasses image authentication, as well as a denial-of-service. A 2048-byte out-of-bounds write was reproduced under AddressSanitizer (sz=4096, off=4096, ih_hdr_size=6144).

On releases before v2.0.0 (v1.9.0 and v1.10.0) the destination is a file-scope static uint8_t buf[SOC_FLASH_ERASE_BLK_SZ] in .bss rather than the stack VLA described above — the code then lived in boot/zephyr/single_loader.c, before commit c9fa6088 relocated it to boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c and changed the buffer's storage class. The out-of-bounds write is equally real and equally pre-authentication on those releases, but it corrupts adjacent static data rather than the stack, so a stack-smashing proof of concept written against a current release will not reproduce as-is there.

Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code IntegritySwati KhandelwalNov 24, 2026Vulnerability / Windows Security

A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so […]

text:
WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without LoginSwati KhandelwalNov 24, 2026Web Security / Vulnerability

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation.

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon.

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.
Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.
Update to a fixed release.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The critical vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.
CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored.

"N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity."

CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement.

The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China.
"In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step."

Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server.

"In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root."

Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network.

CVE-2026-134068 - Stack-based buffer overflow in replication origin name parsing in AWS pgactive

Bulletin ID: 2026-198-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:00 AM PST

Description:

pgactive is an open source PostgreSQL extension from AWS that provides active-active replication between PostgreSQL databases.

We identified CVE-2026-134068, an issue in the replication origin name parsing component of pgactive. Under certain circumstances, an authenticated database user with specific privileges might be able to execute arbitrary operating system commands as the database operating system user.

Impacted versions: >= 2.1.0 AND < 2.1.10

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in pgactive version 2.1.10. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Until upgrading, ensure pgactive.pgactive_conflict_handlers is empty on every node and prevent new inserts. Also use only pgactive generated replication slot/origin names and never malformed, manually renamed, or overlong names. On pgactive 2.1.0, also revoke EXECUTE on pgactive.pgactive_parse_replident_name from PUBLIC.

CVE-2026-134066 - Query injection via schema-derived identifiers in Graph Explorer

Bulletin ID: 2026-199-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:30 AM PST

Description:

Graph Explorer is an open-source tool for browsing and searching graph data, which customers self-host against Amazon Neptune or other graph databases.

We identified CVE-2026-134066, an issue in the query construction of Graph Explorer before version 3.2.1. Graph Explorer inserted property keys and labels read from the connected graph database into Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL query text without escaping. A user with write access to the connected graph database could create a crafted property key or label that, when another user performs a search, causes Graph Explorer to run unintended query logic that accesses and modifies data in that database with Graph Explorer's privileges. On Amazon Neptune, the SPARQL path is not affected.

Impacted versions: < 3.2.1

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in Graph Explorer version 3.2.1. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

If you cannot upgrade immediately, restrict write access to the graph database that Graph Explorer connects to so that only trusted principals can create or modify property keys and labels.

title: Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar
text:
Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar

November 24, 2026

Key Points

Check Point Research identified Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iranian threat group linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Based on our observations, we believe this is the first Iranian group to designate Cyprus as a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure.

The group uses KuboShell, a new backdoor that utilizes IPFS for command-and-control (C2) functions, to deploy the Homa Framework, a post-compromise framework built on a reimplementation of MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go client. Alongside custom malware, Volant Manticore delivers RMM tools and runs credential-harvesting campaigns.

Further analysis shed light on the operators’ internal setup, including development, testing, and operational environments, both on-premise and in the cloud. We observed the group testing their tooling against antivirus products before deployment, as well as using Fortinet SSL VPN clients which suggests access to the victims’ networks via VPN.

While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster.

Volant Manticore’s targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments. A recent shift toward Saudi Arabian targets, including the healthcare sector, may reflect the escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Introduction

Check Point Research is tracking a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group who we named Volant Manticore. What started in July 2026 as a single backdoor delivered to a Cyprus-based airline through a fake CV has since expanded into a broader cluster of activity that we traced back to September 2025.

MuddyWater is an Iranian espionage group linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), focusing primarily on espionage and active since at least 2017. Volant Manticore shares tooling and tradecraft with MuddyWater, but their narrow regional focus, custom implants, and distinct TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) set it apart.

Cyprus is at the center of Volant Manticore’s operations. The island’s deepening defensive and energy ties with Israel and Greece, and its role as a hub for Western military operations in the region, make it a natural target for Iranian intelligence collection. Cyprus was among the countries where we observed a rise in Iran-nexus targeting of IP cameras starting February 28, 2026, activity that may precede military strikes as well as support post-battle damage assessment. The group’s focus on the island’s telecommunications companies and airlines is consistent with Iran’s history of operational activity against individuals in Cyprus.

In September 2026, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis, we observed Volant Manticore abruptly shifting their attention to Saudi Arabia and targeting healthcare organizations. This fits the MOIS’s track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations.

In this report, we analyze the KuboShell backdoor and the Homa Framework, map Volant Manticore’s wider infrastructure, and analyze an earlier campaign against a likely Cypriot government target. We also cover the group’s recent turn toward Saudi Arabia and present evidence for our attribution.

3 new ways Field Effect MDR strengthens identity security

By Mallory Tretter

“Attackers don’t break in anymore. They log in.”
It’s a familiar line in cybersecurity for a reason. As more work moves to the cloud, a single stolen identity can open the door to email, files, and every app connected to them.
That’s why we’re evolving Field Effect’s cloud security, and fast. In just a few weeks, we’ve rolled out three major enhancements that help organizations prevent, detect, and respond to identity attacks like never before:

Faster threat detection and response: Cloud attacks detected and contained in under two minutes

Why identity security matters more than ever
Identity is now the #1 attack vector, and a large part of that is due to AI. The attacks themselves aren’t new, but AI has made them faster, more scalable, and more convincing.
AI can map org charts to find the right targets, research them for personalized lures, write flawless messages at scale, and even clone voices for convincing deepfakes. Work that once took a skilled attacker weeks can now take minutes. Meanwhile, ready-made phishing kits package these skills together, so even inexperienced attackers willing to pay can launch a polished campaign.
Once inside an organization, attackers are hard to detect. Without the right context, they use legitimate sign-ins and authentication flows to hide in plain sight. A single compromised identity gives them:

Sensitive data: Immediate access to files, records, and shared resources stored in cloud accounts that can be read, exfiltrated, or encrypted.

A trusted mailbox: A real employee’s inbox they can use for business email compromise (BEC), posing as that employee or a vendor to trick others into sending money or data.

A foothold for lateral movement: A working login they can use to access other systems, moving from one account or application to the next across your environment.

That context is what Field Effect MDR provides. It spans endpoint, cloud, network, and now AI, so what we learn in one part of your environment informs protection in the rest. And it's an approach we've been refining for years.

Since then, we've detected thousands of threat actors by identifying malicious and suspicious behavior within that broader context. We’ve continually evolved our defenses to stay ahead of attackers as the stakes have risen, and the surge in AI-powered attacks is no exception.

title: Microsoft reports Entra Connect Health metadata exposure
text:
November 24, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Microsoft reports Entra Connect Health metadata exposure

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

On November 20, 2026, Microsoft began notifying affected tenants that attackers had exploited a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API to access tenant metadata, including administrator and technical contact email addresses.

The vulnerable functionality existed in the Microsoft-hosted service from July 23, 2026, until a service-side fix was deployed on November 19, 2026. No customer patch or agent update is required.

The exposed information can help threat actors identify identity administrators, map hybrid identity deployments, and build targeted phishing or social engineering lures against organizations and managed service providers (MSPs).

Threat summary
On November 20, 2026, Microsoft began issuing security advisory notifications through Azure Service Health after identifying exploitation of a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that allowed unauthorized read-only access to tenant metadata. The vulnerable functionality was introduced on July 23, 2026, detected on November 9, and remediated through a service-side fix deployed on November 19, 2026.
Microsoft Entra Connect Health is the monitoring component of Microsoft's hybrid identity platform. Health and operational data gets sent to the service for monitoring and alerting via agents installed on identity infrastructure, including:

Microsoft Entra Connect synchronization servers

Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain controllers

The vulnerable component was the Connect Health cloud service API. One of its functions, GetTenant, returns tenant contact information and service metadata used for monitoring and agent registration. Under normal operation, this information is available only to authorized users associated with that tenant.
The vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to tenant metadata belonging to other organizations. Information exposed through the API included:

Administrator and technical contact email addresses

Tenant identifiers and names

Domain information

Licensing details

Synchronization status

Onboarding status

Regional information

A certificate previously used by an internal Microsoft service that was retired in 2024.

Microsoft reported that passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, active cryptographic keys, Azure subscription data, and Active Directory infrastructure information were not exposed.
The vulnerability affected the Microsoft-hosted service rather than customer-managed software. Exploitation targeted Microsoft's cloud API and did not require access to customer networks, on-premises systems, or internet-facing identity infrastructure. The version of Microsoft Entra Connect or the installed Connect Health agents did not influence exposure.
Observed activity is currently limited to unauthorized access to tenant metadata. Microsoft reviewed service telemetry, identified affected tenants, and issued notifications through Azure Service Health. Public reporting indicates that multiple organizations and MSPs received notifications affecting one or more customer tenants.
To help organizations determine what information may have been exposed, Microsoft published a read-only PowerShell script that retrieves the tenant metadata returned by the affected API. Microsoft noted that the script reflects current values and may not exactly match the data exposed if tenant information changed after the incident.
Analysis
Organizations using Microsoft Entra Connect Health between July 23 and November 19 of this year may have been affected. Unlike typical identity-related vulnerabilities, exposure was not tied to software versions, internet-facing infrastructure, or deployment decisions. title: The Cyber Threats Behind Space Race 2.0
text:
PUBLISHED ON 24 NOV 2026

Joseph Rooke, Insikt Group®

Summary

The new space race isn't just rockets and lunar bases. From the 2022 Viasat attack to hacktivists blinding Iran's tanker fleet, cyberattacks on ground stations, vendors, and terminals are a serious threat. As Earth’s orbit fills with satellites and possibly even AI data centers, securing space matters as much as reaching it.

BackgroundThere were 329 orbital launch attempts in 2025, up from 263 the year before. In the same year, a record 4,517 satellites were placed in orbit. 87% of these satellites were commercially owned; they are part of a space economy that reached $686 billion in 2025 and is set to skyrocket further.In April 2026, Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby, the first humans beyond low Earth orbit since 1972. In March, NASA paused the Gateway station and pivoted to building a lunar base instead. Beijing expects taikonauts on the Moon's surface by 2030 and a functioning International Lunar Research Station by 2035.The first space race ended with the Cold War, but now that geopolitical competition is escalating, the second space race has begun, and cybersecurity will play a vital role in the outcomes.This is because thousands of new satellites are computers running software written by people. So is every lander, rover, and relay that follows them to the Moon. They also all have a connection to a ground station on Earth, which is connected to the internet. Therefore, as the second space race accelerates, the risk of cyberattacks affecting space operations is rising exponentially year after year.

Figure 1: A Long March-10B carrier rocket takes off from China's Hainan province in July 2026 (Source: CNN)

Commercial Space Becomes the TargetAt around five in the morning on February 24, 2022, roughly an hour before Russian armor crossed into Ukraine, tens of thousands of satellite modems across Europe went dark.Russia had used a weapon called AcidRain, a data-wiping malware tool that targets modems, routers, and satellite communications, to target the KA-SAT broadband network run by Viasat, which the Ukrainian military relied on for command and control. AcidRain was pushed out through the operator's own management network.The collateral damage extended far beyond the battlefield: around 5,800 wind turbines in Germany lost remote monitoring, and ordinary customers from Poland to France lost their internet access. The UK, US, and EU later attributed the attack to Russia.Nobody launched a rocket. Nobody fired a jammer. It was a cyberattack that used satellites.This will be part of the story of the second space race.

Figure 2: A simplified graphic showing the KA-SAT cyberattack (Source: Recorded Future)

Space Operations Have a PostcodeWe imagine satellites as remote and therefore safe; however, they are not.Every satellite has a terrestrial address: the ground stations that command it, the links that carry its telemetry, the user terminals at the edge, and the software supply chain behind it all. That is where attackers go, because that is where the doors are.The doors are often unlocked. Researchers at UC San Diego and the University of Maryland pointed an $800 dish at the sky and found that roughly half the geostationary satellites they could see were transmitting in the clear: telecommunications backhaul, corporate traffic, military communications.In March, the NSA and its Five Eyes partners issued joint guidance warning that as low Earth orbit constellations grow, the attack surface open to adversaries expands across the space, ground, and user segments, as well as the supply chains behind them.

Google has released an emergency security update addressing CVE-2026-134401, a Critical vulnerability in Google Chrome that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code outside the browser sandbox after a victim loads a specially crafted HTML page.

The vulnerability is caused by improper input validation in Chrome’s Variations component and is classified as CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.6 (Critical). Google has not yet disclosed the precise vulnerable function, malformed input structure, or technical exploitation chain because access to the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted while the majority of users receive the security update.

The Chrome Stable channel was updated on November 23, 2026 to versions 158.0.8127.88/.89 for Windows and macOS and 158.0.8127.88 for Linux. Chrome 158.0.8127.92 for Android contains the corresponding security fixes, while the Extended Stable channel for Windows and macOS received version 156.0.8078.114.

The vulnerability is particularly serious because Google’s CVE description states that successful exploitation can potentially execute code outside the Chrome sandbox. Browser sandboxing normally restricts compromised rendering processes from directly accessing the wider operating system, so a flaw capable of bypassing that boundary can significantly increase the impact of a malicious web page.

As of November 24, 2026, Google and the available public reports have not confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks. No campaign-specific attacker infrastructure, malware payloads, or exploit chain has been disclosed.

text: The OpenSourceMalware team discovered two related npm packages, clampony and safeclamp3, that impersonate the legitimate clamp utility. Clampony's install hook points to a JavaScript credential stealer, and that stealer downloads a new-to-us custom Windows backdoor that calls itself "Enterotoxin."Enterotoxin is remote access malware. Once it's running, it:Asks a hard-coded server at 195.123.6.29 for Python and batch scripts and runs whatever it receives, giving its operators arbitrary code execution with the infected user's privilegesLogs keystrokes and watches the clipboardCaptures screenshots across every monitorHides its persistence behind Microsoft Store and Windows Update namesRewrites trusted Windows shortcuts so that opening an everyday app runs the malware firstWhat makes this chain worth a close look is how broken the first stage is. In clampony 1.0.9 through 1.0.11, the preinstall hook downloads the stealer from two mirrored URLs, but never saves or runs it. It would be easy to dismiss it as an unfinished package. But those URLs serve a working stealer that goes after AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, npm, PyPI, Git and SSH credentials, sends them to the operators through Telegram, and downloads Enterotoxin. And because Enterotoxin runs whatever its server sends, the behavior documented in this post is a minimum, not a ceiling.Safeclamp3 1.0.11 copies clamp the same way and registers the same preinstall hook, but only launches a 14-byte placeholder script. It looks like a staged or dormant sibling package, not a second way in.The package relationship, custom malware name, infrastructure, Telegram configuration and development style are useful clustering leads, but we found no evidence that supports attribution to a known actor.TL;DRThreat Type: Multi-stage npm supply chain malware, credential stealer, and Windows backdoorAffected Ecosystem: npmRelated Packages: clampony and safeclamp3Initial Trigger: preinstall lifecycle hookImpact when the second stage runs: Developer and cloud credential theft, arbitrary remote command execution, persistence, keylogging, clipboard capture, screenshots, and shortcut infectionC2: https://195.123.6.29:443Exfiltration: Telegram Bot API for the JavaScript stealer; custom HTTPS tasking protocol for EnterotoxinKey Finding: An npm loader that looks broken leads to a fully featured Windows backdoor that runs whatever Python and batch tasks its server sendsSafeclamp3 Finding: The recovered 1.0.11 build only launches a no-op placeholder, with no network destination, credential collection, or Enterotoxin payload pathAttribution: Unknown; no actor attribution is supported by the available evidenceOverview of the packages and attack chainClampony and safeclamp3 have identical LICENSE.md, README.md, index.js and test.js files. text: CommentCommentsSave StorySave this storyCommentCommentsSave StorySave this storyNvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton. Jensen Huang Was Reinstated. What the Hell Is Going On?The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit. “If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock. OpenAI, Cisco Unveil Shirudo to Block Exploits Before Patches
AI-Powered Linux Shields Aim to Protect Vulnerable Systems While Teams Develop Fixes

Emilia David •
November 24, 2026

Image: Shutterstock

The growing number of vulnerabilities found by artificial intelligence models has given organizations a shorter timeframe to send out patches, even if they use agents to help plug any holes.See Also: 43% Are Piloting Healthcare AI Agents. Just 3% Have Deployed Them
OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo, an open-source approach that creates "shields" to block exploits while security teams roll out their longer-term patches, in a bid to widen that timeframe further. Shirudo, Japanese for "shield," runs on Linux systems.
AI models, particularly the more cyber-capable ones such as OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra or Anthropic's Mythos 5, have surfaced previously unknown vulnerabilities. Already overwhelmed security teams are being encouraged to turn to AI agents to find and patch these issues. Even so, testing and deploying patches still takes days or weeks.
"We're giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow," Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, said in a blog post. "We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open."
OpenAI and Cisco invited other developers, security researchers and infrastructure operators to iterate and contribute to their work on Shirudo.
With Shirudo, security teams can test temporary safeguards "to block the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through." If the test works, the shield can be deployed without bringing the entire system down.
The agent writes a temporary block that sits in front of the vulnerable code and prevents the kind of malicious input the exploit depends on. The shield lets security teams test if the patch works while stopping anyone from accessing it. On Linux, the operating system that Shirudo currently works with, many of those shields run inside the operating system's core using a technology called extended Berkeley Packet Filter, or eBPF.
The agent decides where to intercept the attack and where to place the shield it wrote to block it. The agent generates the patch code and begins testing it while the shield blocks malicious attempts to access the kernel.
OpenAI said it tested Shirudo on the Java4Shell vulnerability. Its team used Codex agents, the same agent platform that helped the research firm Calif find Java4Shell. The lab pointed the agent to do a search on the Elasticsearch platform, which allows users to look data within their system and happens to run on the Java language. The team, using Shirudo, added a shield that will check any input they make to Elasticsearch. When the team attempted to exploit the Java4Shell vulnerability by writing malicious input into Elasticsearch, the shield blocked that attack while the platform kept running.
"When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running," OpenAI said.
Shirudo is an open-source platform licensed under the BSD 2-Clause. Cisco and OpenAI said the goal is to make "tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures" while the open-source community builds out patches.

title: An Unclassified CIA System Was Breached in a Cyberattack, AP Source Says
text:
An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, according to a person familiar with the incident who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity.

The breach did not involve any classified information and the issue has been resolved, said the person, who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on condition of anonymity.

The breach affected a system that handles open source intelligence, which involves the collection and analysis of publicly available data from sources including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers. Though the information is generally public or semi-public, open-source information can give intelligence analysts significant insight on its own or in combination with intelligence obtained from classified spying programs.

It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible.

The breach was first reported by The New York Times on Tuesday.

The incident comes to light following a series of highly disruptive system failures that unnerved many Americans. An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline for a time last week, and the FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains.

Those incidents followed a nationwide ground stop that snarled air travel after air traffic controllers struggled to communicate with pilots. Apple, JP Morgan Chase and Microsoft also had systems go down this month.

The incidents have put a spotlight on the vulnerabilities inside critical infrastructure, banking systems and the digital tools that millions of people use daily.

President Donald Trump’s administration says the series of outages is not part of a coordinated cyberattack and dispatched Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to calm Americans in appearances on Sunday morning news shows.

Clayton said the outages largely stem from the rush to patch and upgrade systems to stay ahead of hackers who are now empowered with sophisticated artificial intelligence tools to attack at an unprecedented scale.

text: Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark ReadingNovember 24, 20262 Min ReadSource: the-lightwriter via Getty Images An infamous cyber-espionage group has added a new trick to its tool belt, in the form of VPN bridge obfuscation.Rapid7 published research concerning Webworm, a China-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) group first reported on in 2022 and believed to be active since at least 2017. Webworm's activity predominately targets government organizations, with an emphasis on Europe. The group has also been tracked as Erudite Mogwai and Space Pirates.Webworm has been known to deploy the open source SoftEther VPN on previously compromised government networks. While SoftEther is a legitimate multiprotocol VPN, threat actors abuse its capabilities in attacks. Webworm actors in particular include a "VPN Bridge" component allowing them to link a victim's internal network directly to attacker-controlled servers to facilitate long-term access.The new research, published on Nov. 19, covers what Rapid7 researcher and blog post author Milan Spinka called "a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence." Rebranding SoftEther as Something More GenericRapid7 has identified a range of samples of the tool, which is internally described as "NtMonitor." The tool is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge compiled for Windows x64 and appears to be specifically designed to disguise legitimate SoftEther VPN software as a benign network monitoring utility so the attacker can maintain long-term, stealthy access to compromised network while evading detection tools made to recognize standard SoftEther software artifacts. At its core, Spinka wrote, it appears the attacker "methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it."Attackers changed the metadata and internal branding to refer to generic "Network Monitor Software," for example. Additionally, they changed internal string references to refer to "NtMonitor VPN" like debug banners, service names, registry pages, and firewall rule names (though this was inconsistently applied); renamed the HTTP endpoints used by the VPN protocol; changed the handshake watermark so standard SoftEther detection signatures wouldn't pick it up; stripped down a core file (hamcore.se2) and embedded it inside the executable; and renamed and encrypted SoftEther's plaintext configuration file with a custom cipher.Defending Against a Webworm AttackRapid7 attributed the software to Webworm with moderate confidence, due to alignment with previously reported Webworm tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), as well as remote IP addresses traced to infrastructure repeatedly linked to Webworm activity in the past. Rapid7's research blog includes indicators of compromise and YARA rules for defenders. Dark Reading contacted Rapid7 for additional information, but the research team was unavailable at press time.One of Webworm's primary initial access methods appears to be exploiting vulnerabilities through external Web-facing applications, based on prior vendor research and the APT's affinity for vulnerability scanner Nuclei. Defenders wary of Webworm should prioritize internet-facing patching, Web Application Firewall (WAF) enforcement, and strict network egress controls. text:
Key takeaways

Tower Records Japan, the music and video retailer, says attackers broke into its online store, Tower Records Online, and took members' data. It found the access at about 17:10 on November 19 and stopped the store.
The largest group is login data: email addresses, member IDs and password hashes for 10,214,652 accounts. Names, birth dates, gender and postcodes leaked for 2,784,514, and delivery addresses and phone numbers for 776,953. Members who left within the last three years are included. No card data was involved.
The notice says the hashes "cannot be read as the original password as is". It does not say how they were hashed, whether Tower Records will reset passwords, or that members should change the same password on other services. It tells them only to beware of suspicious emails.
In our view, that is the missing advice. Ten million email and password-hash pairs are what attackers use for credential stuffing, and how quickly the hashes can be cracked depends entirely on the method the notice does not name.

What happened#
According to Tower Records Japan's notice of November 21, updated on November 22:

Date
Event

Nov 19, about 17:10
Unauthorized access to Tower Records Online confirmed; the service is stopped and put into emergency maintenance

Nov 19 onward
The investigation confirms that customers' personal data leaked

Nov 21
Public notice

Nov 22
Update: web orders to start shipping on November 23; the marketplace stays stopped while the safety of its seller admin site is checked

The store is still closed. The company has not said how the attackers got in, and says it will publish its findings and a restart date later. It has not said whether it has reported to the privacy regulator or the police.
Tower Records Japan has been a separate company from the original US chain since 2002. The breach is on its Japanese site, tower.jp.
What was taken#

Data
Accounts or records

Login data: email address, member ID, password hash
10,214,652

Member data: name, name in kana, nickname, birth date, gender, postcode
2,784,514

Delivery data: address, addressee, phone number
776,953

The headline figure is "about 11 million". It is not the sum of the three groups, which comes to 13.78 million, and the notice does not explain how it was counted. It places the breach among the largest in Japan this year; it is now on our list of 2026's largest breaches.
Members who left within the past three years are included. Keeping former members' data for a period is common, but as we wrote in our article on companies deleting data, every year of retention adds people to a breach who are no longer customers.
The passwords#
The notice's only words on the passwords are a footnote: a hash "cannot be read as the original password as is". That is true of any hash, and it says little about the risk.
What matters is the method. A fast, unsalted hash such as MD5 or SHA-1 lets attackers test billions of guesses per second on ordinary hardware, and common passwords fall in minutes. A salted, deliberately slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2 makes the same work far more expensive, though weak passwords still fall eventually. The notice does not say which Tower Records used, and with ten million hashes in attackers' hands, some passwords will be recovered either way.

# The FBI Made Arrests. The Attackers Came Back Anyway.

There is nothing quite as satisfying for a cybercriminal as a well-timed victory lap. This week, ShinyHunters decided to remind us that they're still here. They didn't just return; they did it with the kind of theatricality that suggests they’ve been watching the FBI’s press releases and laughing.

With 5 stories hitting the wire this week, the group is making a point. After the Department of Justice spent months patting itself on the back for arresting individuals linked to their operations, ShinyHunters has reappeared. Their proof isn't a manifesto or a vague threat. They’re using old PGP keys—the digital equivalent of showing a fingerprint and saying, "I'm still holding the pen."

The incentive here isn't just data theft. It's brand preservation. In the world of high-end extortion and data brokerage, your reputation for reliability is everything. If you're rumored to be in a federal prison, your value on the dark web plummets. By returning now, they aren't just targeting companies; they're targeting the narrative of law enforcement success.

The playbook remains predictably ruthless: find a way in, exfiltrate everything, and wait for the moment where the reveal causes the most friction. We see this same hunger for prestige across the board. Look at Scattered Spider, whose recent $11.6 million crypto theft wasn't just about the money—it was about the sheer audacity of the heist.

But while ShinyHunters plays with PGP keys and ego, the broader environment is getting louder. We’ve seen a massive breach at IDScan that exposed over 150 million documents. We saw the myColorado app go dark after 150,000 residents had their data stolen. Even the energy sector isn't safe, with KEPCO confirming a hit on roughly 1.5 million people.

The attribution here is where things get fuzzy. The FBI wants you to believe that arresting a few key players dismantles a group. That's wishful thinking. Probability suggests ShinyHunters is less of a tight-knit gang and more of a franchise or a loose collective of specialists. When the "head" gets cut off, another cell simply assumes the brand identity because that brand already has the trust of buyers and the fear of victims.

There’s a second-order effect here that nobody is pricing in: the emboldening of the middle class of criminals. Every time a group like ShinyHunters survives a federal crackdown and returns with a smirk, it signals to every mid-tier actor that the risk of arrest is just a temporary PR hurdle. It tells them that as long as you have a backup plan and an encrypted key, the law is essentially a suggestion.

The obvious objection is that these are simply copycats—impersonators using leaked keys to ride the coattails of a famous name. It’s a clean theory. It allows the agencies to keep their victory medals. But copycats usually lack the timing and the specific access levels we're seeing this week. Impersonators steal crumbs; they don't usually orchestrate returns that align so perfectly with the gaps in federal enforcement.

This leads us to the genuinely uncomfortable question: Who actually benefits from an arrest that doesn't stop the attack?

Usually, it’s the people who have to write the press releases. A "significant disruption" looks great on a quarterly report to Congress, even if the disruption lasted exactly three weeks before the actor logged back in from a different VPN. We are prioritizing the appearance of victory over the reality of neutralization.

We've seen this rhyme before. The 2016-era leaks and subsequent "takedowns" often followed the same pattern: a flurry of arrests, a period of silence, and then a return under a slightly different name or with a renewed appetite. The only difference now is that the actors are more comfortable mocking us in real-time.

The FBI can keep the handcuffs. […]

01A month of federal breaches

Hackers broke into an open-source intelligence analysis system used by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and exposed some unclassified information, The New York Times reported, citing U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter. The people said classified material was not put at risk, but they believe information held by other government agencies was also exposed.

According to the Times, the affected network searches public, unclassified material for intelligence insights. That material includes commercially available data sets, social media content and satellite imagery. Officials have not said what specific information was taken, how the intruder got in or how long the access lasted. The people who spoke to the Times said a hacker gained unauthorized access to at least one government system, but they did not say whether investigators know who is responsible.

“Unclassified” does not mean low-value. Open-source intelligence (OSINT) is intelligence built from publicly available sources, and it can include data that agencies buy from commercial data brokers. The Times noted that such purchased data can be highly revealing, especially when it is combined with other data sets. # 11 Million Users Exposed. It Was Just a Record Store.

The weirdest number on the wire today isn't from some government ministry or a bank. It's Tower Records. They reported a breach hitting roughly 11 million users.

For those of us who remember the days of music superstores, this feels like a ghost in a graveyard. But it's very real for people whose data just walked out the door, and the volume is just staggering. When you see a number over 10 million, you usually think of a social network or a global SaaS provider. Seeing it with a music retailer means one of two things: they've been hoarding legacy data from their peak years (without any plan to prune it), or their customer growth outpaced their security budget.

It's the "treasure chest" problem; attackers don't always want the most secure vault; they want the biggest pile of loot with the flimsiest lock. Tower isn't critical infrastructure, but 11 million records is enough fuel for phishing campaigns to last a decade.

Then there's the FBI. They're facing a second breach involving the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database. Now the stakes shift from identity theft to physical safety, and the NCIC is basically the shared brain of US law enforcement, holding records on stolen property and fugitives.

The obvious victim is the FBI's reputation for competence. But the second-order effect hits the beat cop in some random Ohio precinct; if data on "cautionary notes" or who is "wanted" gets leaked, or manipulated, the officer walking into a high-risk situation is relying on blind trust. Once the source of truth goes public, the element of surprise is gone and risk to officers in the field spikes.

The wire is loud today, and there were 99 breach stories reported alone, making for a weekly total of 567, and it makes you want to unplug your rack and move into the woods. But if you look past the noise, the real technical failure is at VMware.

VMware vCenter has another critical authentication bypass flaw (CVSS score of 9.8), and it's already been used as a zero-day. I want to make sure any sysadmins reading this understand what an "authentication bypass" actually means here, since people often confuse it with a "crypto flaw."

Assume any vendor claiming "military-grade" encryption is lying or just doesn't know math. For this vCenter bug, though, the strength of the encryption is irrelevant. An authentication bypass isn't about breaking ciphers or guessing passwords; it's about finding a path through the code where the system simply forgets to ask for your ID.

Imagine a high-security building with biometric scanners and 256-bit encrypted keycards on every door (that's the "military-grade" part). An authentication bypass is realizing that if you push the emergency exit bar in a specific sequence, the side door just pops open, and you didn't pick the lock; you bypassed it entirely.

Claude Shannon (the father of information theory) knew system security depends on the unpredictability of the key. But entropy doesn't help if the software accidentally provides a "back door, and this isn't a crypto failure; it's a failure of state management. The system enters a state where it assumes you're authorized because a check was skipped in the logic flow.

People usually argue that these flaws are inevitable in complex code and that VMware is too big to be bug-free; that's true, but the implication is worse. vCenter is the nervous system of the virtualized data center. If an attacker bypasses authentication there, they aren't just in one server; they have the keys to the kingdom, and they can delete the production environment, steal memory dumps by snapshotting existing VMs, or spin up new ones.

Directrice de recherche à l’IRIS, co-responsable du programme Asie-Pacifique, directrice de l’Observatoire géopolitique de l’Indo-Pacifique

L’accueil réservé à la Première ministre japonaise Sanae Takaichi lors du sommet de la Coopération économique pour l’Asie-Pacifique (APEC) à Shenzhen a illustré la profonde détérioration des relations entre la Chine et le Japon. Entre contentieux historiques, rivalités de puissance en Asie orientale et désaccords croissants autour de Taïwan, les deux voisins traversent l’une des périodes les plus tendues depuis plus d’une décennie. Si l’interdépendance économique empêche encore une rupture totale, la logique de compétition stratégique semble désormais prendre le dessus.

Dès l’arrivée de la Première ministre japonaise Sanae Takaichi, plusieurs détails protocolaires ont été interprétés comme des signes de désapprobation chinoise, voire d’humiliation calculée. L’absence d’accueil cérémoniel comparable à celui accordé à d’autres dirigeants, exception faite du président Donald Triump et de Vladimir Poutine, délibérément mis en avant, a retenu l’attention des médias japonais. Plus significatif encore, Sanae Takaichi n’a obtenu aucun entretien bilatéral avec Xi Jinping, alors que plusieurs chefs de gouvernement de la région, dont le président sud-coréen, ont bénéficié d’échanges directs avec le dirigeant chinois.

Ces « signaux » multiples de Pékin ont transmis un message clair et souligné que l’amélioration de la relation avec Tokyo ne figurait pas parmi les priorités immédiates du régime chinois.

Le poids de l’histoire et de la géopolitique

Les tensions actuelles révèlent la montée des nationalismes régionaux. Côté chinois, cela s’appuie sur un substrat mémoriel largement instrumentalisé. En écho au siècle des « humiliations », l’invasion japonaise de la Chine entre 1931 et 1945 continue de structurer le discours national chinois qui dénonce désormais le « néo-militarisme » de Tokyo. De son côté, le Japon considère souvent que les excuses officielles exprimées à plusieurs reprises depuis les années 1970 ainsi que l’aide publique au développement (APD) accordée à la Chine sont insuffisamment reconnues. Entre 1979 et 2022, Tokyo a fourni à la Chine environ 3 660 milliards de yens d’APD, (soit 23 milliards de dollars, selon le taux de change) principalement sous forme de prêts à taux préférentiels qui ont contribué au financement de grands projets d’infrastructure tels que le métro de Pékin, l’aéroport international de Shanghai-Pudong ou plusieurs installations portuaires. Pourtant, ces initiatives ont peu modifié les perceptions mutuelles des opinions publiques.

Au-delà du passé, ce sont les rivalités géopolitiques contemporaines qui alimentent aujourd’hui la méfiance. Le principal point de friction concerne les îles Senkaku, administrées par le Japon mais revendiquées par la Chine sous le nom de Diaoyu. Depuis la nationalisation de trois de ces îlots par le gouvernement japonais en 2012, les incursions de navires des garde-côtes chinois dans les eaux revendiquées par Tokyo se sont multipliées.

Selon les autorités japonaises, les navires chinois patrouillent désormais presque quotidiennement à proximité de l’archipel. Les avions de combat de la Force aérienne d’autodéfense japonaise réalisent plusieurs centaines d’interceptions par an face aux appareils chinois approchant l’espace aérien de l’archipel. Cette pression aéromaritime s’inscrit dans un contexte plus large de modernisation militaire de la Chine. La Chine a développé une approche pragmatique dans la gestion de son monopole qu’elle considère comme un actif stratégique. Elle entretient une tension suffisante pour en maintenir la force politique, optimiser son rendement économique, tout en évitant une rupture.

Le ministère chinois du Commerce (MOFCOM) et les douanes ont prolongé le 9 novembre la suspension de six mesures de contrôle à l’export. Annoncées le 9 octobre 2025, ces mesures restent gelées jusqu’au 10 janvier 2027. La suspension devait expirer le lendemain.

Les contrôles d’avril 2025 échappent à cette trêve. Ils soumettent à licence sept terres rares moyennes et lourdes, dont le dysprosium et le terbium. Selon S&P Global, ils restent en vigueur. Ces deux métaux sont ceux qui permettent aux aimants des moteurs électriques de conserver leurs capacités magnétiques même dans le cas de fortes chaleurs.

En 2024, la Chine assurait 60 % de l’extraction mondiale des terres rares pour aimants et 91 % de leur raffinage, selon l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Elle produit aussi près de 95 % des aimants permanents. Pékin a mis trente ans à bâtir cette position. Il l’exploite aujourd’hui en gestionnaire.

Une position construite sur trente ans

La construction de l’actif a été planifiée. En 1992, Deng Xiaoping résume l’ambition en une phrase : « le Moyen-Orient a le pétrole ; la Chine a les terres rares ». Le Portail de l’IE rappelait cette formule en 2021, à propos de la hausse de la production chinoise.

Pékin protège également le savoir-faire autant que la matière. En décembre 2023, il interdit l’exportation des techniques d’extraction, de séparation et de fabrication d’aimants. Selon un analyste de Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, cette interdiction complique surtout le démarrage de capacités de séparation des terres rares lourdes hors de Chine.

Sur ce segment, la Chine détient 97 % des capacités mondiales. La matière se vend encore sous conditions, mais plus le procédé pour la traiter.

Gérer la tension plutôt que menacer

Un monopole n’a de valeur que si les autres en ressentent le poids. Sans tension, l’actif devient invisible : les prix hors de Chine rejoignent les prix chinois, le monopole cesse de compter dans les négociations. La stratégie chinoise consiste donc à entretenir une tension permanente, à un niveau choisi.

Sur le plan politique, la tension sert de monnaie d’échange. Dès mai 2025, Pékin accordait quelques licences au moment d’une détente avec Washington. Les analystes y voient la démonstration d’une capacité à piloter les flux de terres rares dans le conflit commercial. Le calendrier des suspensions suit aujourd’hui celui des négociations : Washington a aligné sa propre trêve sur le 10 janvier 2027.

Cette approche politique produit également un bénéfice économique secondaire. Sur les huit premiers mois de 2026, les volumes chinois exportés ont reculé de 11,1 %. Leur valeur a pourtant progressé de 53,5 % sur un an. La tension se convertit en rente : la Chine vend moins et gagne davantage.

A contrario, une tension trop forte fragilise la valeur de l’actif. Les événements de  2010 l’ont montré. Pékin réduit alors ses quotas d’exportation de 40 % et impose au Japon un embargo non déclaré de deux mois après un incident maritime.

Tokyo répond par l’investissement. Le conglomérat Sojitz et l’agence publique Jogmec soutiennent l’australien Lynas, alors seule option hors de Chine. La part chinoise des importations japonaises passe d’au moins 90 % à 60 à 70 %. La rupture a renforcé l’autonomie de l’adversaire et fait perdre à la Chine une part de son monopole.

L’échec est aussi juridique. Saisie par les États-Unis, l’Union européenne et le Japon, l’OMC condamne les quotas chinois en 2014. Selon le panel, ils étaient conçus pour servir […]

title: Extending Supply Chain Security in EU Defence Funding: From Components to Raw Materials
text:
Extending Supply Chain Security in EU Defence Funding: From Components to Raw Materials

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Sandra Mezzadri
ARES Board Member and Scientific Advisor, MSB Consulting srl CEO

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, wider instability and US pressure on Europe to take charge of its own defence have led the EU to commit to defence readiness by 2030. This requires Europe to become as autonomous as possible wherever industrial dependence is critical to its capabilities, a considerable challenge given its long reliance on imports, above all from the United States, and the close integration of its main producers with foreign suppliers.

To reduce this dependence without undermining industrial cooperation that remains essential, the EU has cautiously introduced European preference conditions into its defence programmes. Under EDIP grants and SAFE loans, these are limited to a minimum share of component costs that must be European. Yet the rule stops at the component, leaving out the critical raw materials inside it, although Europe depends almost entirely on third countries, above all China, for several of those most critical to defence. Hence a paradox: a rule designed to reduce dependence on an ally may leave Europe more dependent on a strategic competitor.

China’s 2025 export restrictions on rare earths, gallium and germanium, and the sharp rise in tungsten prices in 2026, show that this dependence already constrains European defence production. Defence readiness therefore also depends on secure access to critical raw materials, and this is the issue the paper sets out to explore.

It first analyses how the exclusion of critical raw materials from EU funding conditions affects the path towards industrial autonomy that EU defence instruments are meant to support. It then assesses whether the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), the RESourceEU Action Plan and the EDIP Security of Supply Regime are sufficient to protect defence supply chains and finds that they improve awareness of dependencies but leave verifying the origin of materials and reducing exposure largely voluntary for companies receiving EU defence funding. Finally, rather than maintaining the status quo, it suggests a realistic way forward for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework: linking EU defence funding more closely to supply chain mapping, supported by emerging origin verification methods, and to diversification wherever viable alternatives exist. Whether such a step is taken will ultimately depend on the Commission’s proposals for the next MFF, and on the readiness of the Council and the European Parliament, as co-legislators, to support them.

Politically, it was timed to cause maximum embarrassment to President Putin, on the eve of his arrival in China for a highly publicised trilateral with Presidents Trump and Xi. Tactically, Ukraine was responding to an earlier Russian attack on the North and South bridges in Kyiv that night. And strategically, the attack raises important questions about Russia’s ability – or not – to regroup its southern supply chains under pressure.This is not the first time the bridge has been attacked, but it is the first time it has sustained such persistent damage. While the piers of the bridge appear largely intact, if cracked, replacing the destroyed steel arch is difficult – the original was constructed on land and floated into place, and there is little to prevent Ukrainian drone attacks from continuing to block attempts to repair it. There might be little utility in repairing the bridge at all, although the Kremlin has already pledged to rebuild it.Displacement and ContainmentAll of Russia’s road, rail and river systems are interdependent, and obstructions to one part of the network naturally have consequences for others. There are probably two different ways of looking at the consequences of this attack for Russia’s southern logistics and military sustainment.First, displacement. In the short term, if the road bridge remains out of commission for several months or even a year, traffic into and out of Crimea will be displaced onto its remaining rail link. That rail bridge itself has come under additional attack since the road bridge was destroyed, further disrupting traffic. Ferries to Crimea were already mostly out of commission anyway, even though Putin claimed to be restarting that service swiftly. That rail bridge is by design restricted in its load-bearing capacity over the Kerch Strait, and cannot accept a sudden significant increase in cargo, meaning it cannot account for the traffic in its entirety required to support the peninsula. A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

Threat actors breached at least three AI inference providers and stole customer prompts, but none detected the intrusions until they were notified, according to cybersecurity firm Dragos.

AI inference providers host AI models and sell access to them through APIs. The hacks were detected after a team led by Dragos chief research officer HD Moore sent out roughly two million prompts to widely used AI services between July and November.

These prompts contained a unique, trackable bait such as URLs, hostnames, and credentials, including AWS keys. The security firm then set up a monitoring system to see whether anyone used the bait information in the wild, which meant the prompt had been compromised.

Dragos soon found evidence indicating that someone had stolen information from one of the tested AI inference providers. “Although our prompts were bait, they were processed along with real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too,” Moore noted.

The biggest breach involved roughly 200 AWS test keys sent to a provider, which were stolen in late October.

“Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran – this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack,” Moore said.

Dragos saw the attackers checking which stolen keys worked, then trying to use them to obtain valuable data from the associated accounts.

The attackers have not been identified, but Dragos said one adversary appears to have hacked two of the providers at the same time, using secrets stolen from both from a single rented server.

OpenRouter, an AI gateway that sends customer requests to dozens of inference providers, was indirectly affected. The company said its own systems were not breached, but it removed three unnamed providers in response to the incident.

OpenRouter also listed security notices published by several providers. It did not say whether these are among the three it removed.

The list includes confidential AI cloud provider Phala, which said an attacker compromised a server running a DeepSeek model served via OpenRouter. It admitted that requests sent between October 21 and November 8 should be considered exposed.

AI cloud platform Together AI revealed that an AI coding agent leaked credentials on GitHub, which were then used to obtain stored prompt samples. Model hosting platform Novita and inference platform Atlas Cloud traced potential exposure to requests that reached the API of model developer MiniMax.

Australian uranium company Peninsula Energy (ASX: PEN; OTCQB: PENMF) has requested a trading halt after a cybersecurity incident hit its uranium mine in the United States.

The incident, the company told the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX), occurred on Friday night and impacted the Lance Project in Wyoming, US.

“The company is undertaking a preliminary investigation of the incident and an assessment of the timing and impact, which will temporarily affect its operations,” Peninsula Energy said in a Monday filing.

According to the filing, the incident resulted in a breach of its “operating system”, while administrative systems in the US and Australia were not affected. It did not specify which technical systems were compromised or whether uranium production had been interrupted.

“Peninsula wishes the trading halt to remain in place until the earlier of the commencement of normal trading on 25 November 2026 or when the company releases the announcement regarding the cybersecurity incident,” the company said.

The wholly owned Lance Project, located in Crook County, relies on in situ recovery to extract uranium, which is then processed into yellowcake, which can be turned into nuclear fuel.
